issues.legal_issue: A factual finding that a contracting party acted as a benamidar cannot be disturbed in a special appeal when evidence supports it.
material_facts: The agreement was in the name of one person, while the Election Tribunal found that the appellant’s father was the real contracting party and the named contractor was his benamidar.
The appellant accepted that there was evidence supporting the Tribunal’s benami finding, although he challenged its weight.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the Tribunal’s finding that the father was the real contracting party and declined to interfere with the benami finding.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a person is a benamidar is a question of fact; a finding supported by evidence is not open to interference in a special appeal. The Court relied on no earlier case for this principle.

predicates.special_appeal: The matter is a special appeal challenging a factual finding made by an Election Tribunal.
predicates.evidence_supports_benami_finding: Evidence supports the finding that the person named in the agreement acted as a benamidar for the real contracting party.

issues.definition: When a special appeal challenges a supported finding that a named contracting party acted as a benamidar, the finding is not disturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A business started by a father is not presumed to be a joint-family business merely because he is the father or manager of the family.
material_facts: The appellant’s father started a new business involving a government contract for felling and transporting timber.
The Tribunal found that the business was a new venture but treated the father’s status as a basis for presuming that the business belonged to the joint family.
The Tribunal did not assess the evidence bearing on whether the father entered the contract for himself or on behalf of the family.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal applied an erroneous presumption; the father’s position did not, by itself, establish that the business or contract was a joint-family concern.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, there is no presumption that a business standing in the name of a family member is joint-family business, even if that member is the manager or father. The father’s debts from a newly started trade may bind his sons under the doctrine of pious obligation, unlike a manager’s debts absent necessity, but that does not make the trade itself a joint-family concern. The Court referred to Ram Nath v. Chiranji Lal, Chhotey Lal v. Dalip Narain Singh, and Hayat Ali Shah v. Nem Chand for the distinction concerning debts. Sections 7(d) and 9(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, make the relevant disqualification depend on the contract being entered into by or on behalf of a joint family, subject to the stated separate-business exception.

predicates.family_business_ownership_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a business or contract belongs to a joint family.
predicates.business_started_by_family_father: The father of family members started the business or venture under consideration.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns family ownership of a business started by a family father, his status alone does not establish that it is a joint-family business.

issues.legal_issue: An election disqualification decision based on an erroneous legal presumption must be reconsidered when material evidence about whether the contract was made for the family was not assessed.
material_facts: The election was challenged on the ground that the returned candidate was interested in a government contract made by his father through a person found to be a benamidar.
The Tribunal declared the election void after presuming, on an erroneous view of Hindu law, that the father’s new business was a joint-family business.
Evidence and circumstances that could support a finding that the father contracted on behalf of the family had not been discussed or resolved by the Tribunal.
The Supreme Court directed reconsideration on the evidence already on record and stated that no further evidence would be allowed.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the Tribunal’s order and remitted the matter for a finding, on the existing evidence, whether the father entered the contract on behalf of the joint family or for his own benefit.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 7(d) and 9(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the relevant disqualification follows where a contract is entered into by or on behalf of a Hindu undivided family; a member carrying on a separate business may fall within the statutory exception if the other family members have no share or interest in that business. The determination therefore required a finding based on the evidence as to whether the father acted for the family or personally. The Court set aside the decision because the Tribunal relied on an erroneous presumption and left relevant evidence unassessed.

predicates.election_disqualification_challenge: A proceeding challenges an election on the ground that the returned candidate was disqualified because of a contract.
predicates.erroneous_legal_presumption: The deciding tribunal treated a legal presumption as establishing a fact necessary for disqualification, although that presumption was not legally available.
predicates.material_evidence_not_assessed: The tribunal did not assess evidence that could establish whether the contracting party acted for the family or personally.

issues.definition: When an election-disqualification decision rests on an unavailable presumption and the tribunal has not assessed material evidence, the decision is set aside and the matter is remitted for a finding based on that evidence.
